facts: The gradient of the secant through $P(c, f(c))$ and $Q(c+h, f(c+h))$ is the difference quotient $m_{\text{secant}}=\dfrac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}$.
As $h\to 0$, $Q$ slides along the curve towards $P$ and the secant turns into the tangent at $P$.
Working out the secant gradient for smaller and smaller $|h|$, such as $0.1$, $0.01$, $0.001$, estimates the tangent gradient at $x=c$.
The gap $h$ may be positive ($Q$ right of $P$) or negative ($Q$ left of $P$), and both give the same limit.

foundation.question_text: For $f(x)=x^2$, find the gradient of the secant line passing through $P(2, 4)$ and $Q(2.5, 6.25)$, where $h=0.5$.
For $f(x)=x^2$, calculate the gradient of the secant line passing through $P(3, 9)$ and $Q(3.1, 9.61)$, corresponding to $h=0.1$.

The table below shows secant gradients $\dfrac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^2$ as $h\to 0$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & 0.1 & 0.01 & 0.001 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & 2.1 & 2.01 & 2.001 \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate the gradient of the tangent to $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=1$.

The table below gives values of $\dfrac{f(4+h)-f(4)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^2$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & -0.1 & -0.01 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & 7.9 & 7.99 & 8.01 & 8.1 \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x)$ at $x=4$.

On the curve $y=x^2$, points $P(2, 4)$ and $Q(2+h, (2+h)^2)$ define a secant line.
Describe what happens to the secant line $PQ$ as $h$ approaches $0$.
foundation.solution_text:
As $h\to 0$, point $Q$ moves along the curve towards point $P$.
The secant line rotates to become the tangent line to the curve at $P(2, 4)$.

foundation.question_text: On the graph of $y=f(x)$, state the geometric meaning of the expression $\dfrac{f(3+0.4)-f(3)}{0.4}$.
foundation.solution_text: The expression represents the gradient of the secant line passing through $(3, f(3))$ and $(3.4, f(3.4))$.

foundation.question_text: For $f(x)=x^3$, approximate the tangent gradient at $x=1$ by evaluating the difference quotient $\dfrac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ with $h=0.1$.
For $f(x)=x^2+2$, approximate the gradient at $x=2$ using the difference quotient with $h=0.01$.

development.question_text: For $f(x)=x^2$, find the gradient of the secant line through $P(-3, 9)$ and $Q(-3.1, 9.61)$, where $h=-0.1$.
For $f(x)=x^3$, find the gradient of the secant through $P(2, 8)$ and $Q(2.05, 8.615125)$, where $h=0.05$.

The table below lists values of $\dfrac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^3$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & 11.994 & 12.006 & 12.06 & 12.61 \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate the value of the derivative $f'(2)$.

The table below lists values of $\dfrac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^4$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & 3.994 & 4.006 & 4.0604 & 4.641 \\\hline\end{array}$
Estimate the instantaneous gradient of $y=x^4$ at $x=1$.
For the concave-up parabola $y=x^2$, explain why secant gradients for $h>0$ at $x=1$ are slightly greater than the true tangent gradient of $2$.
development.solution_text:
Because the curve bends upwards (concave up), the curve between $x=1$ and $x=1+h$ steepens.
The secant line connecting $(1, 1)$ to $(1+h, (1+h)^2)$ therefore has a steeper gradient than the tangent at $(1, 1)$.

development.question_text: Explain why substituting $h=0$ directly into $\dfrac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}$ fails to compute the tangent gradient.
development.solution_text:
Substituting $h=0$ gives $\dfrac{f(c)-f(c)}{0}=\dfrac{0}{0}$, which is undefined.
The gradient must be found as a limit as $h\to 0$ rather than by direct substitution of $0$.

development.question_text: For $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=5$, expand the difference quotient $\dfrac{(5+h)^2-5^2}{h}$ algebraically and evaluate it for $h=0.01$ to estimate the gradient.
For $f(x)=2x^2$ at $x=3$, simplify the difference quotient $\dfrac{2(3+h)^2-2(3^2)}{h}$ and evaluate it at $h=0.05$.

mastery.question_text:
A table of difference quotients $\dfrac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^n$ shows values approaching $32$ as $h\to 0$.
Given that the limiting gradient is $n(2)^{n-1}=32$, determine the integer power $n$.
For $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=3$, compare the one-sided difference quotient with $h=0.1$ to the symmetric difference quotient $\dfrac{f(3+0.1)-f(3-0.1)}{2(0.1)}$.
For $f(x)=x^3-x$, evaluate the difference quotient at $x=2$ with $h=0.01$ to approximate the tangent gradient.
